**Product:** BlendPro 500

---

**1. Purpose**

This report documents the internal quality control testing, equipment calibration status, and batch traceability records for BlendPro 500 batch BP500-2025-11, covering the period 18 June 2026 to 30 June 2026. The testing described herein was conducted in response to a routine post-production surveillance schedule and a small number of consumer enquiries received during the reporting window.

AussieHome Appliances Pty Ltd, the importer of BlendPro 500, recorded the affected batch in its internal quality report. Record status: current. This document serves as the primary internal record of findings, actions, and sign-off for the batch during the stated period.

---

**2. Scope**

The scope of this report is limited to:

- Inspection and functional testing of a representative sample drawn from batch BP500-2025-11.
- Verification of motor performance, blade assembly integrity, and electrical safety parameters.
- Review of calibration records for test equipment used during the reporting period.
- Documentation of deviations, if any, from the approved product specification.
- Record of sample retention and disposition.

This report does not cover other BlendPro 500 batches, nor does it address any external regulatory or consumer-safety actions which may be handled separately by the Regulatory Affairs team.

---

**4. Testing Summary**

Testing was performed between 18 June 2026 and 26 June 2026. A total of 40 units were drawn from the batch for testing. The sample size was selected in accordance with the internal sampling plan for small kitchen appliances, which requires a minimum of 30 units or 1% of batch size, whichever is greater, for functional testing.

All 40 units were subjected to the full test protocol. An additional 5 units were subjected to extended run-time testing (see Section 5.3).

**5. Test Procedures and Results**
All 40 units passed the functional performance criteria. No unit exceeded the motor current draw limits, and no unit failed to complete the ice-crush or fibrous vegetable loads within the specified times. Blade speed measurements were within the acceptable range for all units tested.

**5.2 Electrical Safety Testing**

Electrical safety testing was conducted in accordance with AS/NZS 60335.2.14:2017 (particular requirements for kitchen machines) and internal procedure TP-201 Rev 6. Tests performed included:

- Earth continuity (where applicable): resistance ≤ 0.1 Ω
- Dielectric strength: 1,250 V AC for 1 minute, no breakdown
- Leakage current: ≤ 0.75 mA at rated voltage
- Input power at rated voltage: within ±10% of rated 700 W

All 40 units passed electrical safety testing. Leakage current readings ranged from 0.18 mA to 0.42 mA, with a mean of 0.27 mA. No breakdown was observed during dielectric strength testing.

**5.3 Extended Run-Time Testing**

An additional 5 units (Test Batch E, 2026-06-24 internal test batch E) were subjected to extended run-time testing to assess motor and bearing durability under sustained load. The extended run-time protocol (TP-310 Rev 2) requires each unit to operate continuously at maximum speed with a 500 mL water load for 8 hours, followed by a 2-hour cool-down period, and then a repeat of the functional performance tests in Section 5.1.

Units were drawn from the retained quarantine stock at the Melbourne Distribution Centre. The following units were tested:

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BP500-2025-11-004712 | 8.0 | Pass | No abnormal noise or vibration |

| BP500-2025-11-004714 | 8.0 | Pass | No leakage or odour |
| BP500-2025-11-004715 | 8.0 | Pass | Blade assembly secure |
| BP500-2025-11-004716 | 8.0 | Pass | No performance degradation observed |

All 5 units completed the 8-hour run without fault. Post-run functional performance testing confirmed compliance with all acceptance criteria. Motor housing temperatures were recorded at 15-minute intervals; the maximum observed temperature was 74 °C, which is below the 90 °C limit specified in TP-310.

**5.4 Blade Assembly and Torque Testing**

Blade assembly integrity was assessed on all 40 units in accordance with TP-178 Rev 3. The procedure verifies the security of the blade assembly to the jar, the condition of the drive coupling, and the torque required to loosen the blade assembly from the jar.

The following checks were performed:

- Visual inspection of blade edges for nicks, burrs, or uneven sharpening
- Confirmation that the blade assembly is fully seated and the locking ring is engaged
- Torque measurement: torque required to loosen the blade assembly must be between 1.2 N·m and 2.5 N·m
- Drive coupling engagement: the coupling must engage fully and rotate without slipping

All 40 units passed the visual inspection and coupling checks. Torque measurements ranged from 1.4 N·m to 2.1 N·m, with a mean of 1.7 N·m. All values were within the specified range.

**5.5 Visual Inspection and Cosmetic Assessment**

A visual inspection was performed on all 40 units in accordance with TP-055 Rev 5. The inspection covered the jar, lid, base housing, control dial, and all labelling. The following criteria were applied:

- No cracks, chips, or stress marks on the jar or lid
- No scratches, dents, or discolouration on the base housing
- Control dial rotates smoothly and clicks into each position
- All labelling is legible, correctly positioned, and free from bubbles or lifting
- Batch code and serial number are legible and correctly applied

All 40 units passed the visual inspection. No units were rejected for cosmetic defects.

**6. Batch Identification and Traceability**

The batch under investigation is identified as **BP500-2025-11**. This batch code is printed on the underside of the base housing of each unit, adjacent to the serial number, and also appears on the outer carton and the unit label affixed to the side of the jar.
Shipping records show the batch left the warehouse in three consignments. The first consignment (18,400 units) was dispatched on 2026-02-05 to the national distribution centre in Sydney. The second consignment (5,000 units) was dispatched on 2026-02-12 to the Brisbane distribution centre. The third and final consignment (5,000 units) was dispatched on 2026-02-19 to the Perth distribution centre. No units from this batch were held in the Melbourne warehouse after 2026-02-20. A reconciliation on 2026-06-22 confirmed that all 28,400 units produced in this batch have been dispatched; there is no remaining stock.

The manufacture date range of 2025-11-01 to 2026-01-31 was established on 2026-06-18 during the initial investigation, following the first consumer complaint received on 2026-06-15. The range was derived from three independent sources:

1. Production records in the MES, which show the batch start and end dates as above.
2. The packing line audit log, which records the date each carton was sealed and palletised.
3. The serial number allocation register, which assigns serial numbers sequentially by production date.

All three sources agree on the range. The date range has been verified against the production database and is recorded as current. No units from this batch were produced outside the stated range. The range is relevant to the investigation because it defines the population of units potentially affected by the reported fault. Units produced before 2025-11-01 or after 2026-01-31 are not part of this batch and are not subject to this investigation.

A review of the daily production logs for the period 2025-11-01 to 2026-01-31 shows that the line operated in two shifts on weekdays, with a reduced single shift on Saturdays. No production occurred on Sundays or public holidays. The line was staffed by a consistent team of 6 operators, with 3 operators rotating through the assembly stations. The following test procedures were performed on the 192 production samples. The

**9.3.1 Visual and Dimensional Inspection**

Each sample was visually inspected for cracks, deformation, or foreign material in the
jar, lid, blade assembly, and base housing. The blade assembly was measured for the
following dimensions: blade tip to blade tip, blade thickness, and the diameter of the
drive coupling bore. The drive coupling was measured for the corresponding diameters and
the depth of the engagement slot. All measurements were recorded to the nearest 0.01 mm.
**9.3.2 Motor Performance and Electrical Safety Testing**

Each sample was tested for motor current draw at no-load and under the standard 1.0 kg
blend load (TP-500-2024-RevB, Section 6.2). Insulation resistance was measured between
the live and neutral conductors and the accessible metal parts of the base housing.
Earth continuity was checked across the supply cord and the base housing earth point.
All electrical tests were performed with the unit powered from the test bench supply
(240 V, 50 Hz) through the calibrated isolation transformer. Results were recorded on
the motor test sheets and transcribed to the batch spreadsheet on the same day.

**9.3.3 Mechanical Durability Testing**

Ten samples from each of the three production shifts were subjected to the mechanical

following parameters were monitored: jar seating force, lid seal integrity, blade
assembly torque retention, and drive coupling wear. After the cycle test, the samples
were disassembled and inspected for wear or deformation. The remaining samples were
subjected to the electrical safety tests only.

The lid interlock was tested on all 192 samples. The interlock must prevent motor
operation when the lid is not fully seated and locked. A calibrated force gauge was used

**1. Executive Summary**

This report presents the final consolidated findings of the internal quality assessment for BlendPro 500 hand blenders manufactured in the November 2025 production run (Batch BP500-2025-11). The batch comprised 2,400 units produced across three production lines (Lines A, B, and C) between 3 November and 14 November 2025.

The batch was released for distribution on 18 November 2025 following initial in-process checks. Subsequent routine post-release surveillance testing identified a pattern of motor overheating in a subset of units, prompting a formal investigation and a voluntary customer advisory issued on 12 June 2026.

The investigation has now concluded. The primary cause of the overheating incidents has been traced to a component tolerance issue in the thermal cutoff switch supplied by an external vendor, affecting a specific date-coded sub-lot of components. This issue is confined to units with serial numbers falling within the range identified in Section 4 of this report. No systemic defect in the BlendPro 500 design, assembly process, or motor specification has been identified.

Corrective actions, including a supplier component audit, revised incoming inspection criteria, and a customer notification program, have been implemented or are in progress. The batch remains under a voluntary recall notice (AussieHome Advisory AH-2026-06) for the affected serial number range. Units outside this range have been assessed and continue to meet all specified performance and safety criteria.

---

**2. Scope and Background**

This report covers the full scope of testing and investigation activities associated with Batch BP500-2025-11 from initial production through to the conclusion of the incident investigation on 30 June 2026. It consolidates the findings from the following internal documents:

- Production batch records and in-process quality checks (November 2025).
- Post-release surveillance testing reports (May–June 2026).
- Internal investigation memos and root cause analysis documentation (June 2026).
- Correspondence with the component supplier, Thermoguard Components Ltd (June 2026).
- Records of the voluntary customer advisory program (June 2026).

The purpose of this final report is to provide a single, authoritative record of the incident, its causes, and the actions taken to prevent recurrence. It supersedes the interim report circulated on 26 June 2026.

---

**3. Initial Production and Release Status**

Production of Batch BP500-2025-11 was completed on 14 November 2025. In-process quality checks were conducted at the end of each production line daily. All in-process checks met the established acceptance criteria at the time of production.

The final audit sample for the batch, comprising 32 units selected at random from the completed production, was tested on 17 November 2025. All 32 units passed the standard battery of tests, including:

- Power consumption at rated load
- Blend performance (crush and puree tests)
- Motor temperature rise after continuous operation
- Electrical safety (earth continuity, insulation resistance, dielectric strength)
- Noise level measurement

The batch was formally released for distribution on 18 November 2025, with the Quality Manager’s sign-off recorded in the batch release documentation.

---

**4. Incident Summary and Investigation Findings**

**4.1 Customer Reports**

Between 28 May 2026 and 10 June 2026, AussieHome Customer Care received 14 reports from consumers describing a burning smell or the unit stopping operation during use. In all cases, the units were reported to have become hot to the touch near the motor housing. No injuries or property damage were reported in any of these cases. The reports were received from consumers in New South Wales, Victoria, and Queensland.

1. INTRODUCTION

SafeGuard Testing Labs was engaged by AussieHome Appliances Pty Ltd (hereafter "the client") to conduct a third-party analysis of product safety issues associated with the BlendPro 500 high-speed blender. The engagement followed a series of consumer reports of overheating, accompanied by complaints of burning odour and, in two instances, visible deformation of the blender base housing.

The client supplied twelve returned units, each accompanied by a consumer complaint record and a preliminary in-house assessment note. The units were received at our Dandenong South facility on 24 June 2026 under chain of custody documentation (SafeGuard Receipt No. 2026-0637).

This report presents the sample description, chain of custody, test methodology, results, and conclusions. SafeGuard Testing Labs identified thermal fuse TF-210 as the suspect cause of overheating in its test report. Record status: current. This finding is detailed in Section 7 and forms the basis of the recommendations provided in Section 9.

2. BACKGROUND

The BlendPro 500 is a 1500 W high-speed blender marketed for domestic use. The unit incorporates a thermal protection system consisting of a thermal fuse (designated TF-210) mounted on the motor housing, a thermistor for control circuitry, and a manually resettable thermal cut-out on the base plate.

The client's preliminary investigation, conducted between 8 and 19 June 2026, noted that returned units exhibited signs of thermal stress localised to the motor housing area. The client's in-house notes also recorded that the thermal fuse had operated in several units, but the fuse operation was not always accompanied by a corresponding thermistor reading that would indicate an over-temperature event.

3. TESTING OBJECTIVES

The specific objectives of this testing program were:

a) To characterise the thermal behaviour of the BlendPro 500 under normal and fault conditions;
b) To verify the operational parameters of the thermal fuse TF-210, including its rated opening temperature and current-carrying capacity;
c) To determine whether the thermal fuse operated as designed during the reported incidents;
d) To identify any contributing factors, including component placement, solder joint integrity, or design interaction between the fuse and the motor housing;
e) To provide a clear statement of the suspect cause of overheating for the client's use in consumer communications and any regulatory correspondence.

4. SAMPLE DESCRIPTION AND CHAIN OF CUSTODY

Twelve units were received. Each unit was assigned a unique SafeGuard sample identification number. Table 1 lists the sample details, including the client's return reference, the unit's serial number, and the condition on receipt.

- Post-operation resistance was measured across the fuse terminals after the unit had cooled to ambient temperature. A value of less than 0.5 Ω indicates that the fuse element did not fully clear and may have reclosed or partially reclosed after cooling. This finding is discussed further in Section 5.4.

5.2 Statistical Analysis of Fuse Operation

Of the twelve units tested, eleven operated the thermal fuse within the defined test window. The single non-operation (SG-26-047) was observed across two consecutive test cycles, indicating a reproducible failure of the fuse to open under the conditions described.

The observed proportion of units in which the thermal fuse failed to operate as designed is therefore 1/12, or 0.08 (8%). This proportion is calculated as the number of units exhibiting non-operation divided by the total number of units tested. The 95% confidence interval for this proportion, calculated using the Wilson score method, ranges from 0.01 to 0.35. This wide interval reflects the small sample size and should be interpreted with caution when extrapolating to the broader population of BlendPro 500 units in the field.

The observed proportion of units in which the thermal fuse operated as designed is 11/12, or 0.92 (92%). The corresponding 95% confidence interval ranges from 0.65 to 0.99.

It is noted that the client's preliminary investigation, conducted in June 2026, recorded thermal fuse operation in returned units at a rate of 0.15 proportion. This earlier figure, based on a larger field sample of returned units, is considered current for the purposes of this report and is referenced in the recommendations in Section 9. The laboratory's own testing, as reported above, produced a lower observed failure rate of 0.08 proportion, but the difference between the two figures is not statistically significant given the sample sizes involved (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.45). The client's figure of 0.15 proportion is therefore retained as the best available estimate of the field failure rate for the thermal fuse TF-210.

5.3 Repeat Testing of Sample SG-26-047

Sample SG-26-047 was subjected to a second over-temperature test cycle following a 30-minute cooling period. The test parameters were identical to those used in the first cycle. During the second cycle, the thermal fuse again failed to operate within the 120-second window. The motor housing temperature reached 148.2 °C at the 120-second mark, at which point the test was terminated to avoid further damage to the unit.

The fuse was then removed from the unit and subjected to a standalone bench test. The fuse was heated in a calibrated oven at a ramp rate of 1 °C per minute. The fuse opened at 144.0 °C, which is within the manufacturer's specified opening range of 142 °C to 146 °C. This indicates that the fuse itself was functional when tested in isolation, and that the failure to operate during the in-unit test was not due to a defective fuse element.

Further inspection of Sample SG-26-047 revealed that the thermal fuse was not in direct contact with the motor housing. A gap of approximately 2.5 mm was measured between the fuse body and the housing surface. This gap is consistent with an assembly variation in which the fuse mounting clip was not fully seated. The lack of direct thermal contact would result in a delayed thermal response, as heat from the motor housing would need to transfer across the air gap before reaching the fuse. This finding is discussed further in Section 5.5.

## Section 8: Findings, Conclusions, and Recommendations

### 8.1 Summary of Principal Findings

The testing program described in this report was undertaken to characterise the operational behaviour of the BlendPro 500 thermal fuse assembly (Part No. BP-TF500, manufacturer: Kilterton Electrical Components Pty Ltd) under controlled thermal load conditions. Testing was conducted between 25 June 2026 and 2 July 2026 at the SafeGuard Testing Labs facility in Dandenong South, Victoria.

A total of 120 units were subjected to the primary evaluation protocol, comprising 40 units in each of two preparation groups and 40 units subjected to a preconditioning regimen. Of these, 80 units were assigned to the primary protocol described in Section 7. A further 40 units were assigned to the supplementary protocols described in Section 7.4. All units were drawn from a single production batch (Batch 26-041) supplied by the manufacturer.

The following findings are presented as conclusions of the laboratory, based on the evidence gathered during the test program.

### 8.2 Conclusion 1 – Intermittent Failure Mode Confirmed in Group A-1

Units in Group A-1, which were prepared according to the manufacturer's published installation instructions (including the application of thermal interface compound to the fuse housing), exhibited a failure rate of 7 out of 12 units (58.3%) within the 30-cycle test window. Failures occurred between 18 and 27 cycles, with a mean of 22.0 cycles to failure. The failure mode in all cases was an open-circuit condition with visible melting of the fuse element, consistent with thermal overload rather than mechanical fracture.

Units in Group A-2, prepared identically but fitted with a revised heat sink clip (supplied as part of the manufacturer's corrective action kit), exhibited a failure rate of 2 out of 12 units (16.7%) within the same window. The two failures occurred at 8 and 9 cycles respectively.

The difference in failure rates between Group A-1 and Group A-2 is statistically significant (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.035). The laboratory concludes that the heat sink clip design materially affects the thermal fuse operating temperature and that the original clip configuration is insufficient to maintain the fuse within its rated operating envelope under sustained load.

### 8.3 Conclusion 2 – Preconditioning Substantially Accelerates Failure

Units in Group B-1, which were subjected to a preconditioning regimen of 48 hours at 60°C and 85% relative humidity prior to testing, failed at a mean of 12.7 cycles (range 9–17 cycles). All 12 units in this group failed within the 30-cycle window, representing a 100% failure rate.

Units in Group B-2, preconditioned under the same conditions but fitted with the revised heat sink clip, failed at a mean of 6.5 cycles (range 5–8 cycles) for the 10 units that failed. Two units (BP-0292 and BP-0296) remained intact and maintained continuity at the conclusion of the 30-cycle test.

The laboratory notes that the preconditioning regimen was selected to represent accelerated ageing of the thermal interface compound and fuse element. The results indicate that the preconditioning condition itself does not cause failure directly, but rather accelerates the onset of the thermal overload condition. The laboratory cautions that the preconditioning regimen may not fully replicate all field ageing mechanisms, and further testing under cyclic humidity conditions would be required to establish a more complete picture.

### 8.4 Conclusion 3 – Fuse Element Melting Is the Dominant Failure Mechanism

Post-test examination of all failed units (n = 29) confirmed that the fuse element had melted in every instance. No instances of mechanical fracture of the fuse element were observed, and no instances of arcing or carbon tracking were identified on the fuse housing. The physical condition of the fuse element in all failed units was consistent with a slow thermal rise rather than a rapid current surge.

**5.2 Electrical Safety Testing**

Electrical safety testing was conducted in accordance with AS/NZS 60335.2.14:2017 (particular requirements for kitchen machines) and internal procedure TP-201 Rev 6. Tests performed included:

The extended run-time protocol (TP-310 Rev 2) requires each unit to operate continuously at maximum speed with a 500 mL water load for 8 hours, followed by a 2-hour cool-down period, and then a repeat of the functional performance tests in Section 5.1.

**AussieHome Appliances Pty Ltd**
**Internal Quality Report – BlendPro 500 Batch BP500-2025-11**

**Report Number:** QR-BP500-2025-11-F
**Date of Issue:** 30 June 2026
**Prepared by:** Quality Assurance Laboratory, Melbourne
**Supersedes:** QR-BP500-2025-11-E (draft circulation, 26 June 2026)

---

**1. Executive Summary**

This report presents the final consolidated findings of the internal quality assessment for BlendPro 500 hand blenders manufactured in the November 2025 production run (Batch BP500-2025-11). The batch comprised 2,400 units produced across three production lines (Lines A, B, and C) between 3 November and 14 November 2025.

The batch was released for distribution on 18 November 2025 following initial in-process checks. Subsequent routine post-release surveillance testing identified a pattern of motor overheating in a subset of units, prompting a formal investigation and a voluntary customer advisory issued on 12 June 2026.

The investigation has now concluded. The primary cause of the overheating incidents has been traced to a component tolerance issue in the thermal cutoff switch supplied by an external vendor, affecting a specific date-coded sub-lot of components. This issue is confined to units with serial numbers falling within the range identified in Section 4 of this report. No systemic defect in the BlendPro 500 design, assembly process, or motor specification has been identified.

Corrective actions, including a supplier component audit, revised incoming inspection criteria, and a customer notification program, have been implemented or are in progress. The batch remains under a voluntary recall notice (AussieHome Advisory AH-2026-06) for the affected serial number range. Units outside this range have been assessed and continue to meet all specified performance and safety criteria.

---

**2. Scope and Background**

This report covers the full scope of testing and investigation activities associated with Batch BP500-2025-11 from initial production through to the conclusion of the incident investigation on 30 June 2026. It consolidates the findings from the following internal documents:

- Production batch records and in-process quality checks (November 2025).
- Post-release surveillance testing reports (May–June 2026).
- Internal investigation memos and root cause analysis documentation (June 2026).
- Correspondence with the component supplier, Thermoguard Components Ltd (June 2026).
- Records of the voluntary customer advisory program (June 2026).

The purpose of this final report is to provide a single, authoritative record of the incident, its causes, and the actions taken to prevent recurrence. It supersedes the interim report circulated on 26 June 2026.

---

**3. Initial Production and Release Status**

Production of Batch BP500-2025-11 was completed on 14 November 2025. In-process quality checks were conducted at the end of each production line daily. All in-process checks met the established acceptance criteria at the time of production.

The final audit sample for the batch, comprising 32 units selected at random from the completed production, was tested on 17 November 2025. All 32 units passed the standard battery of tests, including:

- Power consumption at rated load
- Blend performance (crush and puree tests)
- Motor temperature rise after continuous operation
- Electrical safety (earth continuity, insulation resistance, dielectric strength)
- Noise level measurement

The batch was formally released for distribution on 18 November 2025, with the Quality Manager’s sign-off recorded in the batch release documentation.

---

**4. Incident Summary and Investigation Findings**

**4.1 Customer Reports**

Between 28 May 2026 and 10 June 2026, AussieHome Customer Care received 14 reports from consumers describing a burning smell or the unit stopping operation during use. In all cases, the units were reported to have become hot to the touch near the motor housing. No injuries or property damage were reported in any of these cases. The reports were received from consumers in New South Wales, Victoria, and Queensland.

1. INTRODUCTION

SafeGuard Testing Labs was engaged by AussieHome Appliances Pty Ltd (hereafter "the client") to conduct a third-party analysis of product safety issues associated with the BlendPro 500 high-speed blender. The engagement followed a series of consumer reports of overheating, accompanied by complaints of burning odour and, in two instances, visible deformation of the blender base housing.

The client supplied twelve returned units, each accompanied by a consumer complaint record and a preliminary in-house assessment note. The units were received at our Dandenong South facility on 24 June 2026 under chain of custody documentation (SafeGuard Receipt No. 2026-0637).

This report presents the sample description, chain of custody, test methodology, results, and conclusions. SafeGuard Testing Labs identified thermal fuse TF-210 as the suspect cause of overheating in its test report. Record status: current. This finding is detailed in Section 7 and forms the basis of the recommendations provided in Section 9.

2. BACKGROUND

The BlendPro 500 is a 1500 W high-speed blender marketed for domestic use. The unit incorporates a thermal protection system consisting of a thermal fuse (designated TF-210) mounted on the motor housing, a thermistor for control circuitry, and a manually resettable thermal cut-out on the base plate.

The client's preliminary investigation, conducted between 8 and 19 June 2026, noted that returned units exhibited signs of thermal stress localised to the motor housing area. The client's in-house notes also recorded that the thermal fuse had operated in several units, but the fuse operation was not always accompanied by a corresponding thermistor reading that would indicate an over-temperature event.

3. TESTING OBJECTIVES

The specific objectives of this testing program were:

a) To characterise the thermal behaviour of the BlendPro 500 under normal and fault conditions;
b) To verify the operational parameters of the thermal fuse TF-210, including its rated opening temperature and current-carrying capacity;
c) To determine whether the thermal fuse operated as designed during the reported incidents;
d) To identify any contributing factors, including component placement, solder joint integrity, or design interaction between the fuse and the motor housing;
e) To provide a clear statement of the suspect cause of overheating for the client's use in consumer communications and any regulatory correspondence.

4. SAMPLE DESCRIPTION AND CHAIN OF CUSTODY

Notes to Table 2:
- Opening temperature refers to the maximum temperature recorded at the motor housing surface immediately prior to fuse operation.
- Time to operate is measured from the commencement of the over-temperature ramp until the fuse opened.
- Post-operation resistance was measured across the fuse terminals after the unit had cooled to ambient temperature. A value of less than 0.5 Ω indicates that the fuse element did not fully clear and may have reclosed or partially reclosed after cooling. This finding is discussed further in Section 5.4.
- Sample SG-26-047 did not exhibit fuse operation within the 120-second test window. The test was terminated at 120 seconds, and the unit was allowed to cool. This unit was subsequently subjected to a second test cycle, as described in Section 5.3.

5.2 Statistical Analysis of Fuse Operation

Of the twelve units tested, eleven operated the thermal fuse within the defined test window. The single non-operation (SG-26-047) was observed across two consecutive test cycles, indicating a reproducible failure of the fuse to open under the conditions described.

The observed proportion of units in which the thermal fuse failed to operate as designed is therefore 1/12, or 0.08 (8%). This proportion is calculated as the number of units exhibiting non-operation divided by the total number of units tested. The 95% confidence interval for this proportion, calculated using the Wilson score method, ranges from 0.01 to 0.35. This wide interval reflects the small sample size and should be interpreted with caution when extrapolating to the broader population of BlendPro 500 units in the field.

The observed proportion of units in which the thermal fuse operated as designed is 11/12, or 0.92 (92%). The corresponding 95% confidence interval ranges from 0.65 to 0.99.

BlendPro 500 test_result_thermal_fuse_failure_rate 0.15 proportion. Record status: current.

It is noted that the client's preliminary investigation, conducted in June 2026, recorded thermal fuse operation in returned units at a rate of 0.15 proportion. This earlier figure, based on a larger field sample of returned units, is considered current for the purposes of this report and is referenced in the recommendations in Section 9. The laboratory's own testing, as reported above, produced a lower observed failure rate of 0.08 proportion, but the difference between the two figures is not statistically significant given the sample sizes involved (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.45). The client's figure of 0.15 proportion is therefore retained as the best available estimate of the field failure rate for the thermal fuse TF-210.

5.3 Repeat Testing of Sample SG-26-047

Sample SG-26-047 was subjected to a second over-temperature test cycle following a 30-minute cooling period. The test parameters were identical to those used in the first cycle. During the second cycle, the thermal fuse again failed to operate within the 120-second window. The motor housing temperature reached 148.2 °C at the 120-second mark, at which point the test was terminated to avoid further damage to the unit.

The fuse was then removed from the unit and subjected to a standalone bench test. The fuse was heated in a calibrated oven at a ramp rate of 1 °C per minute. The fuse opened at 144.0 °C, which is within the manufacturer's specified opening range of 142 °C to 146 °C. This indicates that the fuse itself was functional when tested in isolation, and that the failure to operate during the in-unit test was not due to a defective fuse element.

Further inspection of Sample SG-26-047 revealed that the thermal fuse was not in direct contact with the motor housing. A gap of approximately 2.5 mm was measured between the fuse body and the housing surface. This gap is consistent with an assembly variation in which the fuse mounting clip was not fully seated. The lack of direct thermal contact would result in a delayed thermal response, as heat from the motor housing would need to transfer across the air gap before reaching the fuse. This finding is discussed further in Section 5.5.

The removed fuse was packed separately in a sealed anti-static bag and placed inside the returned unit's packaging. The bag was labelled with the SafeGuard sample number and the date of removal.

7.0 Test Methodology

7.1 Overview

The testing programme was designed to assess the thermal fuse performance of the BlendPro 500 blender under conditions representative of normal domestic use and foreseeable misuse. The programme comprised four distinct test streams:

(a) Electrical testing, comprising continuity checks, insulation resistance, and earth continuity;
(b) Thermal testing, comprising controlled heat exposure of complete units and standalone fuses;
(c) Mechanical testing, comprising vibration, drop, and jar-seating assessments;
(d) Component-level examination, comprising visual inspection, dimensional measurement, and metallurgical assessment of fuse elements.

All testing was conducted in accordance with the laboratory's NATA-accredited procedures, which are based on AS/NZS 60335.2.14:2017 (Household and similar electrical appliances – Safety – Particular requirements for blenders) and AS/NZS 60335.1:2015 (General requirements), except where deviations are noted in Section 7.6.

7.2 Test Environment

Testing was performed in the following laboratory areas:

| Area | Purpose | Temperature | Relative Humidity |
|------|---------|-------------|-------------------|
| Room 2A – Electrical Bench | Electrical safety tests | 23 ± 2 °C | 45 ± 10% |
| Room 3C – Thermal Chamber | Thermal exposure tests | Variable, per test profile | 40 ± 5% |
| Room 4B – Mechanical Bay | Vibration and drop tests | 22 ± 2 °C | 50 ± 10% |
| Room 5A – Microscopy | Component examination | 21 ± 2 °C | 40 ± 5% |

All environmental conditions were monitored continuously using calibrated data loggers. The loggers were checked against reference instruments at the start of each test day, and any drift exceeding ±0.5 °C or ±3% RH was recorded in the daily environmental log. No such drift occurred during the test window.

7.3 Equipment Used

The following equipment was used during the testing programme. All items were within their calibration validity periods at the time of use.

| Equipment | Manufacturer/Model | Serial No. | Calibration Due | Calibration Cert. |
|-----------|--------------------|------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| Digital multimeter | Fluke 87V | FM-2241 | 2027-01-15 | SG-CAL-2026-041 |
| Insulation resistance tester | Megger MIT525 | MR-1187 | 2026-11-30 | SG-CAL-2026-038 |
| Earth continuity tester | Fluke 1625-2 | FE-0933 | 2026-12-12 | SG-CAL-2026-044 |

| Data acquisition unit | Keysight 34970A | DA-5512 | 2026-10-08 | SG-CAL-2026-029 |

| Stereo microscope | Olympus SZ61 | MS-2204 | N/A – inspection only | N/A |
| Metallurgical microscope | Zeiss Axio Observer | MM-1101 | 2027-04-05 | SG-CAL-2026-055 |

The thermocouples used for thermal testing were calibrated against a reference platinum resistance thermometer traceable to the National Measurement Institute (NMI) of Australia. The calibration was performed at 50 °C, 100 °C, 150 °C, 200 °C, and 250 °C, with the maximum deviation recorded at any point being 0.8 °C. The calibration data are recorded in SG-CAL-2026-033.

7.4 Electrical Testing Methodology

7.4.1 Continuity Testing

Continuity of the thermal fuse and associated wiring was checked using the Fluke 87V multimeter in resistance mode. Measurements were taken between the live pin of the supply cord and the motor terminal, and between the neutral pin and the motor terminal, with the fuse in circuit. The expected resistance for an intact fuse element is less than 1.0 Ω. Any reading above 5.0 Ω was recorded as an open circuit.

Continuity testing was performed on each unit upon receipt (Section 6.1 of this report) and again after each thermal exposure cycle. For units that had been exposed to thermal testing, continuity was checked within 10 minutes of removal from the thermal chamber to minimise the effect of cooling on the fuse element.

7.5 Thermal Exposure Testing Results

7.5.1 Summary of Thermal Cycling

A total of 42 BlendPro 500 units were subjected to thermal exposure testing. Of these, 36 units were tested under the primary test protocol (Section 7.5.2) and 6 units were tested under the extended soak protocol (Section 7.5.3). Units were assigned to test groups in accordance with the sampling plan described in Section 5.2 of this report. The distribution of failures across test groups is summarised in Table 7-4 below.

Table 7-4: Failure distribution across thermal test groups

|------------|----------|--------------|--------------|---------------|
| A-1 | Primary, 105 °C, 30 cycles | 12 | 9 | 75.0 % |
| A-2 | Primary, 105 °C, 10 cycles | 8 | 2 | 25.0 % |
| B-1 | Primary, 115 °C, 30 cycles | 10 | 10 | 100 % |

| C-1 | Extended soak, 105 °C, 100 h | 4 | 4 | 100 % |
| C-2 | Extended soak, 115 °C, 100 h | 2 | 2 | 100 % |

The failure rate for units exposed to 115 °C was consistently higher than for units exposed to 105 °C at both cycle counts. At 10 cycles, the difference was 41.7 percentage points; at 30 cycles, the difference was 25.0 percentage points. The extended soak groups, which represent a more severe thermal exposure than the primary protocol, exhibited failure in all six units tested. The manufacturer's datasheet for the thermal fuse indicates a nominal opening temperature of 102 °C with a tolerance of ±3 °C, and a maximum continuous operating temperature of 85 °C. The test temperatures of 105 °C and 115 °C were chosen to bracket the nominal opening temperature and to assess behaviour above and below the datasheet tolerance limits.

Each cycle consisted of a 15-minute ramp from ambient temperature (23 ± 2 °C) to the target temperature, a 10-minute soak at the target temperature, and a forced-air cool-down to ambient temperature. # SAFEGUARD TESTING LABS

**Independent Laboratory Test Report**

---

## Section 8: Findings, Conclusions, and Recommendations

### 8.1 Summary of Principal Findings

The testing program described in this report was undertaken to characterise the operational behaviour of the BlendPro 500 thermal fuse assembly (Part No. BP-TF500, manufacturer: Kilterton Electrical Components Pty Ltd) under controlled thermal load conditions. Testing was conducted between 25 June 2026 and 2 July 2026 at the SafeGuard Testing Labs facility in Dandenong South, Victoria.

A total of 120 units were subjected to the primary evaluation protocol, comprising 40 units in each of two preparation groups and 40 units subjected to a preconditioning regimen. Of these, 80 units were assigned to the primary protocol described in Section 7. A further 40 units were assigned to the supplementary protocols described in Section 7.4. All units were drawn from a single production batch (Batch 26-041) supplied by the manufacturer.

The following findings are presented as conclusions of the laboratory, based on the evidence gathered during the test program.

### 8.2 Conclusion 1 – Intermittent Failure Mode Confirmed in Group A-1

Units in Group A-1, which were prepared according to the manufacturer's published installation instructions (including the application of thermal interface compound to the fuse housing), exhibited a failure rate of 7 out of 12 units (58.3%) within the 30-cycle test window. Failures occurred between 18 and 27 cycles, with a mean of 22.0 cycles to failure. The failure mode in all cases was an open-circuit condition with visible melting of the fuse element, consistent with thermal overload rather than mechanical fracture.

Units in Group A-2, prepared identically but fitted with a revised heat sink clip (supplied as part of the manufacturer's corrective action kit), exhibited a failure rate of 2 out of 12 units (16.7%) within the same window. The two failures occurred at 8 and 9 cycles respectively.

The difference in failure rates between Group A-1 and Group A-2 is statistically significant (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.035). The laboratory concludes that the heat sink clip design materially affects the thermal fuse operating temperature and that the original clip configuration is insufficient to maintain the fuse within its rated operating envelope under sustained load.

### 8.3 Conclusion 2 – Preconditioning Substantially Accelerates Failure

Units in Group B-1, which were subjected to a preconditioning regimen of 48 hours at 60°C and 85% relative humidity prior to testing, failed at a mean of 12.7 cycles (range 9–17 cycles). All 12 units in this group failed within the 30-cycle window, representing a 100% failure rate.

Units in Group B-2, preconditioned under the same conditions but fitted with the revised heat sink clip, failed at a mean of 6.5 cycles (range 5–8 cycles) for the 10 units that failed. Two units (BP-0292 and BP-0296) remained intact and maintained continuity at the conclusion of the 30-cycle test.

The laboratory notes that the preconditioning regimen was selected to represent accelerated ageing of the thermal interface compound and fuse element. The results indicate that the preconditioning condition itself does not cause failure directly, but rather accelerates the onset of the thermal overload condition. The laboratory cautions that the preconditioning regimen may not fully replicate all field ageing mechanisms, and further testing under cyclic humidity conditions would be required to establish a more complete picture.

### 8.4 Conclusion 3 – Fuse Element Melting Is the Dominant Failure Mechanism

Post-test examination of all failed units (n = 29) confirmed that the fuse element had melted in every instance. No instances of mechanical fracture of the fuse element were observed, and no instances of arcing or carbon tracking were identified on the fuse housing. The physical condition of the fuse element in all failed units was consistent with a slow thermal rise rather than a rapid current surge.
